title: Show HN: Bloque – Hosted MCP gateway for teams without an IT department
summary: Bloque is a hosted MCP gateway for teams without an IT department. There are many MCP gateway products out there, but they are either overkill or too difficult to use. The pricing of a popular product starts at $500/mo, another one requires you to have your own infrastructure, and so on. As the owner of a small company, I encourage my team members to use AI and MCP servers in their daily work, but don't want to waste time helping them set them up. I also need to manage and monitor how they use them. With Bloque, I set up MCP servers once, issue API keys for my team members, and let them connect Claude, ChatGPT, or any tool of their choice to Bloque's single endpoint. That part is easy. Then, I can manage and monitor who calls which tool, when. Bloque started as a fork of the MIT-licensed Plugged.in. We kept the MCP-related core, removed everything else, and rebuilt it as a multi-tenant hosted gateway. Other features include: - Teams - Isolated runtime environments (where stdio-based servers run) - Per-user 3LO: each team member can call MCP servers with their own credentials - Enable/disable tools It's a freemium service: - Free (shared runner, no MCP Playground) - Starter: $5/mo (shared runner) - Pro: $25/mo (dedicated runner) - Team: $29/mo includes 2 seats, $7/mo per additional seat (dedicated runner, team management) I would love feedback, especially from our target audience: one-person IT admins at SMEs. title: Show HN: bouncemarket – a live prediction market game for a bouncing ball
summary: a ball will fall. trade on where it lands. I made this game! Some technical details: The entire drop of the ball is simulated server-side, then streamed to each client as server-sent events with a small buffer. Every drop is deterministic from its starting position, so rounds can be replayed exactly for later analysis, but tiny variations in starting position can change the ultimate outcome. There's some AI traders to keep the market moving, but they drop out in any round that has more than five people. They operate using a naive set of rules that I wrote for them, so they're not too hard to beat -- it's when the market is full of real people that it gets tricky. Curious to get feedback on anything you would change, and especially whether the mechanics were clear right away or not. title: Show HN: GPT Plays Civilization
summary: Hey HN, I've always been a big fan of the Civ games, and was always frustrated at how terrible the AI was. So I got curious about whether LLMs could play Civ well, or not! I thought about having the agents interact with the GUI directly, but something about that seemed like the wrong approach. For one thing, it seemed to me like images would cost way more in tokens. For another, LLMs seem like a different kind of intelligence from humans, so why would an interface meant for humans be optimal for them? Anyway, I spend a few weeks modifying Unciv [0], an open-source reimplementation of Civ V to have the right endpoints and views for an agent to be able to play civ in the same way a person could. title: Show HN: Europe Instead – find the European version of the tools you use
summary: Hi HN, I'm Rafael. Europe Instead is a directory of European-made software: https://europeinstead.com I built it because every time we needed a new tool at my startup, Upgrid, I ended up doing the same research again: who actually owns this company, where is the data hosted, who are the subprocessors. After doing that enough times I got tired of it and started writing it down properly. The existing "EU alternatives" lists didn't help much, because most check one thing, the legal seat. A company registered in Berlin can be owned by a US parent, run on AWS us-east-1, and send your data to a dozen US subprocessors. That is a different risk from a Berlin company on Hetzner. So every tool gets two separate answers: - Origin score (0-100): how European the company is, from five parts: legal entity, ownership and control, operations, data residency, and openness. Weights are published on the method page. - Exposure level (1-5): which jurisdictions can legally reach the core customer data, based on where it is hosted and who the subprocessors are. Every fact links to the page it came from, with the check date and usually a quoted line. If we couldn't find evidence, the fact is shown as "not verified" and scores zero, rather than being guessed. Right now that is about a quarter of all facts, which tells you something about how little vendors disclose. Some details: - 1,818 tools from 33 countries, across 212 categories, mapped as alternatives to 453 US products (Calendly, Typeform, Intercom, Google Analytics, and so on). - Vendors can correct their record by form or email. Corrections are reviewed by a person and logged in a public change history. - Listing is free and unconditional. No backlink required, and rankings can't be bought. If I ever sell sponsored slots, they sit above the ranked list with their own numbering and a "Sponsored" label; the ranking below always starts at 1 and doesn't move. A few things you might find useful: - "Alternative to X" pages: name the tool you use today and see the European ones that do the same job. - Stacks: a full European set of tools for a small company, one per job. - A read-only API and an MCP server, so you can ask an AI assistant for a European alternative and get the sourced record back ( https://europeinstead.com/developers ). - A free badge vendors can embed. It links to their live record and has no tracking. What I'd like from you: tell me where the data is wrong, and tell me where the method is wrong. In particular I'm unsure how to treat the UK and Switzerland (included, country always shown so you can apply a stricter definition), and whether "uses AWS Frankfurt" should count against a tool as much as it does now. title: Show HN: Open-Sourced Code Mode to Cut ~60% of My Rust Agent's Token Burn
summary: For those who are tracking, Anthropic released an announcement last week about their experimental code mode for Claude Code, claiming some bonkers token savings when it comes to tool calls (95% on some workloads(1)). I haven't benchmarked it myself, but independent studies come in somewhere closer to 60~70% savings (2), but I digress. TLDR; I built an open-source version for the community. Context: I'm writing an AI RPG engine called Spookery, and I immediately wanted to try this technique for myself when I heard of it. Agent deployment is currently dominated by token costs, especially during tool calling (single prompt generating tens or hundreds of tool calls). Unfortunately, it looks like the only ones who are doing this seriously are big agentic products like Claude Code and Codex. So, I thought it'd be fun to try it myself and bring it to you all! The idea of Code Mode is simple but powerful. Instead of passing back tool call results back to the LLM one at a time, let the LLM batch calls by letting it write a short script using your tools. Basically taking 30 trips to the grocery store for 30 items and turning it into one trip to the store with a list in-hand. There's a few near-ish open-source options, but they used TypeScript backends, we're a little boilerplate heavy, and I wanted to have something a little faster and Rust friendly for my game engine. Pydantic's Monty seemed a good candidate--their self-reports are around 5x faster on execution and 100x faster on startup (3). I wouldn't take the numbers to the bank, but it's written on a Rust framework and the python backend is entirely built from Rust too. Anyway, I had a couple of days off unexpectedly. So, I went temporarily insane and built a Rust tool to bring code mode to the greater community for free. In enough days to fit on one hand (and just as many hours of sleep), I came up with the implementation linked. I call it Ghost Mode. It's MIT licensed. It's a drop-in for your agent that already makes traditional tool calls. With ~20 lines of setup, you can convert your existing agent to a Code Mode agent. I hope you get something out of this, and maybe I can save you some money. Considering how limiting token economics are right now, I think this could be a game changer for the industry. If there's interest, I can imagine we can build also add some great new features, language compatibility, and other great things. Thanks for reading :) Sources: (1) https://www.marktechpost.com/2026/11/17/anthropic-claude-cod... (2) https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19123 (3) https://pydantic.dev/docs/monty/get-started/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50665796 Points: 2 # Comments: 2

title: Show HN: Targeted Mutation Testing – Observation-guided mutation testing tool
summary: Hi HN, I built a mutation testing tool that takes a different approach from the conventional one. I'm calling it Targeted Mutation Testing. As AI coding has become more common, mutation testing has become more important. It has helped me a lot personally. But ever since I first learned about it, I've kept wondering if there was a smarter way to do it. Targeted Mutation Testing observes a single test run and generates targeted mutants from what it sees. Of course, observation-guided rules have their own limits, so you can also combine them with classic mutation rules when you want more coverage. This post links to the Rust implementation, which I built first. I also built a JS/TS implementation: https://github.com/t-k/targeted-mutation-ts What's interesting about the JS/TS version is that, by focusing on targeted mutants, mutation testing can become practical for E2E tests. I took inspiration from SEMu, DSpot, the W-method, and Meta's ACH. I listed the links at the end. Would love any feedback. Thanks for taking a look. - Killing Stubborn Mutants with Symbolic Execution (SEMu): https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.02941 - Automatic Test Improvement with DSpot: https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.08330 - Testing Software Design Modeled by Finite-State Machines (W-method): https://doi.org/10.1109/TSE.1978.231496 - Mutation-Guided LLM-based Test Generation at Meta (ACH): https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12862 Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50667811 Points: 1 # Comments: 0

title: Show HN: No-equipment workout generator with 3D-to-2D SVG figures
summary: Hey HN, I built* HIIT Builder ( https://hiitbuilder.app ) because I don't want to get fat. Truly I could just stop there. But for more context, I got tired of hunting for YouTube workout videos that have both good routines and decent music. Turns out most YT workout creators, even the massive ones who could afford a license, have terrible music. So, fk it, I'll build my own workout generator and play my own Spotify playlists instead. So far workouts have been completed across 13 countries (US, Iraq, Bangladesh, Austria, France, Germany, Brazil, Ukraine, Turkey, Netherlands, Spain, Chile, Australia), and someone in the Faroe Islands, either physically or maybe just their VPN, started one too. A few technical details that might be interesting to my fellow nerds here: After a few ugly first prototypes for the stick figures, I ended up using the strategy of modeling every animation as a compact 34-number pose vector (joint angles, abduction, etc.) like a 3D skeleton, then projecting it to a 2D SVG. That way any move can be rendered at any angle without having to re-do any major work. For workout order, instead of pure random shuffles the routine builder runs simulated annealing over a fixed standing/floor block shape. This makes it so that trips to the floor are limited and muscle groups are rotated logically. Rest time is actually rest instead of using that time to get up or get down off the floor constantly. Since one of my main concerns was bringing your own music, there are no audio files at all. I did add countdown beeps though with synthesized chonky square waves so they cut through Spotify. *Full disclosure: Using 'built' nowadays is a dividing term lol. I used AI to write all the code for it. And while I've spent many hours reviewing and tweaking poses over and over until the form cues actually looked right, a few of the moves still have noticeable quirks that AI is bad at noticing. If you spot any weird ones let me know. Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50666506 Points: 1 # Comments: 0

title: Show HN: Scolast – AI tutor for autodidacts inspired by Bloom's 2 sigma problem
summary: I was using Claude to learn physics and I was getting a bit frustrated with the interface (I kept interrupting the conversation to get a quick explainer on something, and there was no good interface for Claude to ask me questions) so I built Scolast! It's an AI tutor that follows Bloom's findings ( https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloom%27s_2_sigma_problem ) that 1 to 1 tutoring, using mastery learning (basically only moving ahead when the student has demonstrated they learned something, but also moving ahead as quickly as possible) can have pretty incredible results, around two standard deviations higher than regular classroom learning. Bloom called it a problem because this was obviously untenable - but it's actually possible now! I also added little side explainers for anything that's confusing, plus worksheets, and I've been iterating on the voice of the tutor, to try to get a sort of Feynman-y focus on the whys and the experiments and experiences that motivated each piece of knowledge. I find that it's quite remarkable, I'm actually retaining some of the physics I've never been able to retain in the past, and it seems useful in a lot of other domains - my wife used it for language learning and to pass a yoga exam; I've used it to learn some machine learning subjects, etc. One interesting side effect is that I find using it quite tiring, and I actually use tokens very slowly compared to agentic coding - when you actually have to read every token carefully you really get your money's worth. Would love to get people's thoughts so I'm throwing in $3 in free tokens while my budget lasts. After that you can buy tokens and I'm charging an extra 10% to cover everything else. Eventually I'd like to hook it up to people's existing subscriptions, I've applied to OAI's program for this, waiting to see if Ant will offer it. Cheers Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50661473 Points: 1 # Comments: 0

title: Show HN: SoundEtch, an open source podcast/media editor for the browser
summary: I've been working on this project for a few years, and thinking about it for a few more years. Ever since the pandemic when I did my entire job on a little Chromebook with browser-based tools; why not make an Audacity for the browser? Well, it turned out there were already a few "Audacities for the Browser" like https://audiomass.co/ (posted here a couple times already), https://naomiaro.com/waveform-playlist/ , and a literal Audacity compiled to WebAssembly https://wavacity.com/ . SoundEtch is kind of a beefed up version of those. I made it with podcasters and other spoken-word creators in mind, rather than musicians, since there are a number of browser DAWs already e.g. OpenDAW. Everything is streamed to and from disk (OPFS), with an optional cloud backup. You can close or crash the browser tab, even in the middle of recording, and your data is still there when you open it back up. This also means you can load huge files; my parents' desktop with 8gb RAM handled this 5 hour stereo mp3 I found on archive https://archive.org/details/2023-09-08/2023-09-10.mp3 . There's a transcription-based editing tool like you get with Riverside and Descript. Mine uses IBM's Granite Turbo model, plus some Codex/Claude tweaking to get word-level timestamps. The result is, to my knowledge, much faster and more accurate than any other browser/local ASR out there. It has a few quirks, though, like only emitting lower-case letters and spaces. I also added a WebRTC meeting room with up to 4 guests. It doesn't have a TURN service, so some networks will block you from connecting. Since AI coding assistants are so good these days, I was able to add video support pretty easily. You can import, export, and record video, add that transcript with the current word highlighted, etc. The editing is pretty basic for now: you can trim the clips, move them around, add some effects including noise removal from DeepFilterNet ( https://github.com/Rikorose/DeepFilterNet ). I appreciate your taking a look and any feedback you have! The code is at https://github.com/bfbsoundetch/SoundEtch Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50668765 Points: 1 # Comments: 0

title: Show HN: Blur – a Mac app that hides secrets during screen sharing
summary: Hi HN! We built Blur for a moment you’ll recognize. You’re sharing screen on the call and open some app or file to show something, and accidentally discover that you also demo your API tokens. Blur detects credentials as they appear and blurs just that part of the screen. The rest stays readable, so you can keep walking someone through the file. You can also hide entire apps from the screen share. Detection runs entirely on your Mac. We use CoreML to run MobileNetV4 on Apple’s Neural Engine. Your screen content stays on your machine. Blur doesn’t ask for a username, an ID, or any other personal information. It only connects to the network to check for app updates. There is optional support for Jev-like networks, but it is disabled by default. If you try it, we’d love to hear how it works for you.
